He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

Scenario:
AITA For Selling My Former Roommates Games | So a few years ago I was renting this place with this dude and we were on a lease. When the lease was nearing it's end he just peaced out. We're talking took most of everything leaving only the last bit of his half of rent and a few things he said in a note he didn't want to bring with him. Thing with where I live is that if you don't discard of things on your own when you move out the landlord can pay to have someone remove the stuff. We're talking cases of dudes having $250 taken off their deposit just for some dude to take 3 milk crates of things to the dump. It's a rip off. I texted and emailed him for 2 weeks asking to pick these things up or take them to the dump but he never responded. So I took most of his things to the dump but he also had around 60 video games for PS4. So I figured I'd sell them. There is a local game store where they buy used games and they gave me $600 for all of his games. Well cut to last week and I was at a party he was at and we were polite. He then asks how the move out was and I said good, and naturally he asked what I did with his stuff. He got mad when he found out I sold his games but I told him that I tried to get him to grab these things but he never reached out. He's now calling me an asshole and asking me to pay him back. I checked and legally there's nothing there but now I'm wondering if I'm the asshole for doing this.

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (YTA - You're the asshole)** Here's why, legally and ethically: ### ** Legal Perspective (Most U.S. jurisdictions):** - **You are not the landlord**. Abandoned property laws almost always require the *landlord* to handle unclaimed items, not co-tenants. - **Standard procedure**: Landlords must typically: (1) Notify the tenant in writing (via certified mail) about abandoned property, (2) Securely store it for a legally mandated period (e.g., 30–60 days in most states), (3 ONLY THEN sell or dispose of it *through official channels* (e.g., public auction), with proceeds going toward storage costs or returned to the tenant. - **You bypassed all of this**. By selling the games yourself for $600 profit, you essentially *stashed* someone else's property and kept the proceeds. This could legally qualify as **" conversion"** ( civil theft) or even **" larceny"** in some states. - **" I tried to contact him" is not enough**. The law doesn't empower co-tenants to unilaterally dispose of or profit from another tenant's belongings. Your responsibility was to *notify the landlord*, not take matters into your own hands. ### ** Ethical Perspective:** - **" I don't want to bring these with me" ≠ " I give you permission to sell them"**. The note only indicated he didn't * want* the items—he didn't explicitly transfer ownership or authorize you to profit from them. - **$600 is a significant profit**. If you genuinely believed the items were abandoned, the ethical move would have been to: - Return them to the landlord (who would then follow legal procedures), - or donate them (not sell for personal gain). - *Keep the $600* is the core issue here. It transforms a " well-intentioned but misguided" act into a clear violation of trust. - **" I didn't want to get charged $250 for the dump" is not a valid excuse**. The $250 deposit fee is the landlord's problem to resolve—not yours to " solve" by profiting from someone else's property. ### ** Why This Matters:** - **You created a legal liability for yourself**. The roommate could sue you for the $600 (plus potential damages). - **You violated the roommate's property rights**. Abandonment doesn't mean " free for all"— it means the *landlord* must handle it per state law. - **" I texted him for 2 weeks" is irrelevant**. The law doesn't care about your effort if you're not the legally designated authority (i.e., the landlord). ### ** What You Should Do Now:** - **Apologize and offer to return the $600** (or split it if you genuinely believe he abandon it). - **Next time**: Immediately notify the *landlord* about unclaimed items. Let * them* handle it per lease terms and local law. - **Never profit from someone else's property**— even if they " left it behind." **Final verdict: YTA**. You overstepped legally and ethically by selling the games for personal gain. The fact that you " checked and legally there's nothing there" is almost certainly incorrect—you likely *did* break the law. Consult a local tenant rights attorney if the roommate pursues this further. *(Source: U.S. state abandoned property laws, e.g., CA Civil Code § 1980–1988, NY Real Property Actions & Proceedings Law § 1301, TX Property Code § 92.008)*.
